oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 18 Nov 2026 19:39:58 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 The Key Numbers I’m Watching As Anthropic Makes Its IPO Debut https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/anthropic-ant-ipo-revenue-growth-risks-s1-analysis/ Wed, 18 Nov 2026 19:39:58 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94421 Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1 , the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record. Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology. By the numbers Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets: The company has a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion for compute. Of that, $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030. Anthropic currently has over $100 billion on its balance sheet. Its IPO seeks to add another roughly $100 billion, creating a war chest for those compute commitments. When it launched Claude in the first quarter of 2023, Anthropic had zero revenue. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension. The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization ’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services. That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses. Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption. The offering promises to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is slated to begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares, bringing in about $66.4 billion. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, the IPO and private placement total more than $92 billion. As we revolutionize the way people manage their expenses, being part of the Expensify team means building the easiest, fastest, and most efficient platform to automate everything expense-related.</p> <div>&nbsp;</div> <h2>Customer Success Management at Expensify</h2> <p>Own a portfolio of our mid-market and enterprise customers, from onboarding through renewal and growth. You'll be the person enterprise customers trust to keep things running, and to spot the next opportunity before they've even asked. If you like turning usage data into revenue outcomes and holding your own in a C-suite conversation, this one's for you.</p> <div>&nbsp;</div> <p>As a Customer Success Manager, your responsibilities include:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Building trusted relationships with senior stakeholders across finance, IT and operations, right up to the C-suite</p> </li> <li> <p>Owning the full account lifecycle, from onboarding through adoption, renewal and growth</p> </li> <li> <p>Spotting risk and configuration issues early, and proactively solving them</p> </li> <li> <p>Guiding customers through migrations and product rollouts, instilling confidence in the product and your ability to support them in any software transition within their tech stack</p> </li> <li> <p>Turning usage data into a clear account plan that ties activity back to revenue</p> </li> <li> <p>Driving adoption of Expensify's core products, including expense management, global reimbursement, Expensify Card and Travel</p> </li> <li> <p>Troubleshooting technical issues hands-on, from accounting integrations and card feeds to SSO and API workflows, and tracing each one to its root cause</p> </li> <li> <p>Acting as the bridge between customers and our product and engineering teams, translating customer feedback into something they can act on</p> </li> <li> <p>Managing renewals, upsell and cross-sell conversations, and holding your own in contract talks</p> </li> </ul> <p>You'll be expected to:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Improve net dollar retention across your portfolio</p> </li> <li> <p>Engage with your accounts every quarter</p> </li> <li> <p>Forecast and increase contract renewals</p> </li> <li> <p>Increase product adoption across your accounts</p> </li> </ul> <h2>About You</h2> <p>We're looking for a Customer Success Manager who thinks like a product manager and acts like a trusted advisor. You've owned renewals, run QBRs and grown accounts through cross-sell and upsell. You understand how software works, and financial systems knowledge is a bonus. You're comfortable with data, not vibes, and you build account plans that tie activity back to revenue. You use AI to work smarter, but you never let it replace your own judgment. You see a problem and want to fix it, even when it isn't technically yours to fix.</p> <h3><br>Experience and Background</h3> <p>Required</p> <ul> <li> <p>3+ years of B2B SaaS account management or customer success experience, with direct ownership of a customer portfolio</p> </li> <li> <p>Experience owning renewals, retention, and growth, including commercial conversations around pricing, expansion, or contract terms</p> </li> <li> <p>Strong product and technical fluency, with experience working through APIs, integrations, or other connected software systems</p> </li> <li> <p>Strong data literacy, including using spreadsheets, dashboards, usage data, and reporting tools to make decisions and build a business case</p> </li> <li> <p>Strong written and verbal communication, with the ability to work effectively with both technical teams and senior customer stakeholders</p> </li> <li> <p>Comfort operating autonomously, setting priorities and managing competing demands without heavy day-to-day direction</p> </li> </ul> <p>Desirable</p> <ul> <li> <p>Experience managing enterprise accounts, or a mix of mid-market and enterprise</p> </li> <li> <p>Experience with FinTech, payments, spend management, accounting, ERP, or other financial software</p> </li> <li> <p>Familiarity with tools and integrations such as NetSuite, Okta, Workday, HubSpot, GitHub, Gong, or similar platforms</p> </li> <li> <p>Experience using AI to automate workflows, improve processes, or solve business problems</p> </li> <li> <p>Experience managing global customers and working effectively across time zones and asynchronously</p> </li> </ul> <h2>Compensation &amp; Benefits:</h2> <ul> <li> <p>401(k) with up to 4.5% employer match</p> </li> <li> <p>100% employer-paid medical, dental, and vision coverage</p> </li> <li> <p>$20,000 annual fertility and family-building benefit through Carrot</p> </li> <li> <p>Up to $5,000 in relocation reimbursement if you move to one of our offices</p> </li> <li> <p>Three months of paid parental leave; six months for birthing parents</p> </li> <li> <p>Commuter, healthcare FSA, and dependent care FSA benefits</p> </li> <li> <p>Flexible vacation policy</p> </li> </ul> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/expensify-customer-success-manager">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/expensify-customer-success-manager</a></p> Wed, 18 Nov 2026 21:56:22 +0000 Fri, 18 Dec 2026 21:56:22 +0000 https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/expensify-customer-success-manager https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/expensify-customer-success-manager Luminize: Bilingual Talent Acquisition Specialist / Interviewer (USD Contract) Europe Only Talent Acquisition and Data Entry All Other Remote Full-Time <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Belgrade, Serbia <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="https://luminize.com">https://luminize.com</a> </p> <p><span>🚀 <strong>Be the First Conversation in Every Great Hire</strong></span><br><br>📍 <strong>Role:</strong> Bilingual Talent Acquisition Specialist / Interviewer (USD Contract)&nbsp;<br>📍 <strong>Location:</strong>&nbsp;Belgrade, Serbia&nbsp;<br>&nbsp; The post New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65% appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Hugging Face’s harness-hub team has released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted , a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B . It was trained with reinforcement learning to work inside the pi coding agent . The Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter targets one harness instead of general chat. For developers running local coding agents, that is the point. You keep the open base model and swap in a small, harness-specific adapter. TL;DR Size: LoRA rank 32 (alpha 64) on Qwen3.8-27B, a 27B dense hybrid with 262,144 native context. Merged BF16 checkpoint is about 54 GB. Runs on: vLLM with LoRA enabled, or llama.cpp with a GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base. Inference VRAM is not disclosed. Training used 2x NVIDIA B200. Performance: Large pass@1 gains inside pi with thinking off, plus far shorter sessions. Best: 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), up from 39.2%. Worst: 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The base model with thinking already reaches 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro. Bottom line: Best: thinking-level accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Worst: small eval sets, self-reported, pi only. What is Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted? Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is a PEFT LoRA adapter that turns Qwen3.8-27B into a model tuned for pi. pi is an MIT-licensed agent toolkit with a coding agent CLI. The adapter is released under Apache-2.0 . It applies to the q, k, v, o, gate, up and down projections. It only works on Qwen3.8-27B. The base model is a dense hybrid . It alternates Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention blocks across 64 layers. How does the harness adapter training work? The method comes from Hugging Face’s harness adapters post from November 6. The idea is 1 LoRA adapter per model and harness. Training runs inside the unmodified harness on verifiable tasks. For this checkpoint, the model card lists these details: Algorithm: AsyncGRPO from TRL , 8 rollouts per task at temperature 0.8. Tasks: 750 scale800 tasks interleaved with 300 TermGrade tasks. Reward: verifier correctness plus a tool-efficiency bonus with weight 0.1. Budget: up to 50 agent steps and 1,800 seconds per rollout, thinking off. Checkpoint: step 160. The run stopped at step 191 of 1,000 planned. Every tool call passes through safeagents , a rule-based proxy. It blocks calls such as fetching benchmark answers from the Hub. Blocked rollouts score 0, so RL pushes the model away from reward hacking. Benchmarks: how much does the LoRA adapter help? All numbers below are self-reported. They use the pi harness, 1 attempt per task. Benchmark (pi, thinking off) Base Qwen3.8-27B pi-adapted Change SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 39.2% 64.7% +25.5 ± 14.2 pts (p = 0.0023) Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86 tasks) 39.5% 55.8% +16.3 ± 9.1 pts (p = 0.0013) The adapter solved 15 new SWE-bench Pro tasks and lost 2. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it gained 16 and lost 2. Efficiency is the larger story. On tasks both models solved, median turns fell from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, they fell from 18 to 8. The adapter also generates about 4.5x fewer tokens than the base model with thinking. How does it compare with thinking mode and other adapters? With thinking on, the base model already scores 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. So the adapter matches thinking-level accuracy without paying for long reasoning traces. With thinking on, the adapter reaches 66.7% and 56.6%. Feature Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted Qwen3.8-27B base, thinking on Qwen3.8-27B-opencode-adapted bytkim/Qwen3.8-27B-pi Type LoRA r=32 Base model LoRA r=32 Full fine-tune, 28B Method AsyncGRPO RL None AsyncGRPO RL SFT then GRPO Harness pi pi OpenCode pi License Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 64.7% 64.7% 51.0% (OpenCode) Not disclosed Terminal-Bench 2.1 55.8% 54.2% 53.0% (OpenCode) Not disclosed Token use ~4.5x fewer than base + thinking Baseline ~6x to 8x fewer than base + thinking ~41% fewer output tokens (Terminal-Bench) Training hardware 2x B200 Not disclosed 2x B200 Not disclosed OpenCode adapter numbers use a different harness and are not directly comparable. How do you deploy it? The model card gives 4 routes: vLLM: serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B with --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 32 , thinking disabled. Point pi at http://localhost:8000/v1 . llama.cpp: load the GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base GGUF. Llama.app on macOS: register the adapter with a 32,768-token context. Merge: merge with PEFT on CPU, then serve the 54 GB BF16 result without LoRA flags. Because adapters share 1 base model, a single server can host pi and OpenCode adapters side by side. Key Takeaways Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is an Apache-2.0, rank-32 RL LoRA for the pi agent. SWE-bench Pro hard-51 rises from 39.2% to 64.7%, thinking off. Median turns drop from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. It matches base-with-thinking accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Results are self-reported on small sets; the tweet’s 29.4% baseline was corrected. The post Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Attackers now have powerful AI on their side. AI agents can scan, plan and run intrusions at machine speed, and they improve every month. The result is more attacks, more often and at global scale. In that environment, more companies will face a security incident at some point. What separates them is how they respond. Machine-speed threats call for a modern playbook with 4 pillars. Detect and contain automatically. Communicate fast and securely. Eradicate thoroughly. Keep shrinking the blast radius. This article shows the trend through 6 months of incidents. It then looks at a few companies, with Fireworks AI as a model of mature, structurally sound response. TL;DR The trend: AI-powered attackers are driving more frequent attacks at global scale. The evidence: Several AI platforms disclosed security incidents between May and November 2026. Pillar 1: Detect and contain automatically. Human-speed shutdowns are too slow. Pillar 2: Communicate fast and securely, over out-of-band channels. Pillar 3: Eradicate thoroughly, with outside forensic experts. Pillar 4: Keep shrinking the blast radius. Data that is never stored cannot be stolen. Case studies: Fireworks AI and Klue show these pillars in practice. Why are attacks becoming more frequent? AI has changed the economics of attacking. Tasks that took skilled people days can now be delegated to agents. In November, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said AI misuse had reached a “critical inflection point” . They report that attackers use AI to shorten timelines and run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. CrowdStrike reported that 1 group used AI agents against more than 200 organizations in 11 days . Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 found attacks moving about 4 times faster than a year earlier. The shift started earlier. In 2025, Anthropic disrupted a campaign where AI did 80 to 90% of tactical work with little human input. The tools keep improving, so the pace will keep rising. AI infrastructure is an especially attractive target, because AI access itself has value. The last 6 months show what that looks like. What was disclosed in the last 6 months? Incidents appeared across every layer of the AI stack. Together they show how broad the activity has become. May: package registries. On May 10 and 11, the “Mini Shai-Hulud” campaign altered about 170 npm packages and some PyPI libraries . Affected projects included AI SDKs from Mistral AI and Guardrails AI. The NHS cyber alert lists the specific versions to avoid. June: SaaS integrations. Klue, a market intelligence platform, disclosed misuse of OAuth tokens it held for customers. See case study 2. August: self-hosted AI gateways. Microsoft described intrusions into exposed, unpatched LiteLLM, RAGFlow and Kestra deployments. Fixed versions exist for all 3 tools . CISA had listed the LiteLLM flaw as known exploited on June 8. September: evaluation environments. Anthropic’s September threat report described attempts to obtain AI keys through software vendors. The Cloud Security Alliance summarized it . In 1 case, instructions were injected into a vendor’s automated evaluation sandbox. October and early November: developer platforms. At least 9 AI developer and hosting platforms disclosed incidents involving stored customer secrets in October. Wiz’s tracker later listed further disclosures, for 16 platforms in total. A tampered LiteLLM release, version 1.107.0, was also identified , and users were told to roll back. November: shared web vendors. On November 16, an attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely’s account signup flow to inject code into customer projects, reaching 178 organizations’ websites, according to Report URI, including HSBC, Salesforce, the BBC and Ledger. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses and skimmed payment forms; Optimizely removed the payload and fixed the flaw. Hudson Rock traced similar code through three other web services, beginning November 13. It is the same concentration pattern, one layer below the AI stack. According to the Cloud Security Alliance, entry points varied . The common target was stored environment variables, often holding AI provider API keys. AI keys carry real value, which explains the interest. CSA, citing Anthropic, notes that a key can be resold, used for compute or used as cover . Wiz estimated that misuse of 2 keys from these incidents exceeded $100,000 at list price . That is why spending caps matter. Concentration is the other shared factor. A platform that stores secrets for many customers naturally draws attention. CSA describes this as the platform-chain pattern . What does a modern incident response playbook look like? Detect and contain automatically: A human-speed shutdown is no longer enough. An AI-driven intruder can move between systems in minutes. Mature teams wire detection directly to containment. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:15:36 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Anthropic Prices IPO Shares At $83, Above Range https://news.crunchbase.com/public/ipo/anthropic-prices-ipo-ant-above-range/ Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:15:36 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94423 Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday afternoon, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing, CNBC, Reuters and the Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. The offering promises to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is slated to begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares, bringing in about $66.4 billion. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, the IPO and private placement total more than $92 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX , by comparison, raised $75 billion in its June offering. Fast growth but no profits, yet The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books. For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization ’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services. That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses. Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption. Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:15:36 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.13 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 The Blue Economy: The World’s Quietest Economic Engine And Its Smartest Cities https://news.crunchbase.com/startups/blue-economy-technology-defense-energy-onetti-mind-the-bridge/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:00:45 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94402 By Alberto Onetti The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy. For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources. Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central. Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea. Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge ’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge. Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end. The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end. The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026). Not all blue tech is the same Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups. We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density). The result is a matrix highlighting: Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total). High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech. The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies. Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’ The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy? Short answer: ports. Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy. And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook. To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation. While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy. The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy. To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units. Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges. Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona , a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge . Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them. Get the full story in Mind The Bridge’s report, available for free download here . Alberto Onetti is chairman of Mind the Bridge and a professor at University of Insubria . He is a serial entrepreneur who has started three startups in his career, the last of which is Funambol , among the five Italian scaleups that have raised the largest amount of capital. He is recognized among the leading international experts in open innovation and has wide experience in setting up and managing open innovation projects — venture clients, venture builders, intrapreneurship, CVCs — with large multinational companies, as well as advising and training on this subject.
